==Problem==
A digital display shows the current date as an <imath>8</imath>-digit integer consisting of a <imath>4</imath>-digit year, followed by a <imath>2</imath>-digit month, followed by a <imath>2</imath>-digit date within the month. For example, Arbor Day this year is displayed as <imath>20230428.</imath> For how many dates in <imath>2023</imath> does each digit appear an even number of times in the <imath>8</imath>-digital display for that date?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}~5\qquad\textbf{(B)}~6\qquad\textbf{(C)}~7\qquad\textbf{(D)}~8\qquad\textbf{(E)}~9</imath>

==Solution 1 (Casework)==
Do careful casework by each month. Make sure to start with 2023. In the month and the date, we need a <imath>0</imath>, a <imath>3</imath>, and two digits repeated (which has to be <imath>1</imath> and <imath>2</imath> after consideration). After the casework, we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)}~9}</imath>. 
For curious readers, the numbers (in chronological order) are:

 20230113
 20230131
 20230223
 20230311
 20230322
 20231013
 20231031
 20231103
 20231130

==Solution 2==

There is one <imath>3</imath>, so we need one more (three more means that either the month or units digit of the day is <imath>3</imath>). For the same reason, we need one more <imath>0</imath>. By inspection, we can see that the other two digits must be a repeated digit that is not <imath>3</imath> or <imath>0</imath>. 
 	

If <imath>3</imath> is the units digit of the month, then the <imath>0</imath> must be the units digit of the month, since there is no month ending with 3 that is more than March. In this case, the last two digits must match (<imath>11, 22</imath>). This gives <imath>2023-03-11</imath> and <imath>2023-03-22</imath>, so 2 successes.

If <imath>3</imath> is the tens digit of the day, then <imath>0</imath> can be in any of the remaining three places. If it is in the ones digit of the the day, then the month must be <imath>11</imath>, which gives <imath>2023-11-30</imath>. If it is in the ones digit of the month, then the month must be <imath>10</imath>, in which case the day must be <imath>31</imath>, which gives <imath>2023-10-31</imath>. If <imath>0</imath> is in the tens digit of the month, then the month must be <imath>01</imath>, which gives <imath>2023-01-31</imath>. Together, <imath>2023-11-30</imath>, <imath>2023-10-31</imath>, and <imath>2023-01-31</imath> make 3 successes. 
	

If <imath>3</imath> is the units digit of the day, then <imath>0</imath> could go in any of the <imath>3</imath> remaining slots again. If it's the tens digit of the day, then the other digits must be <imath>1</imath>. If <imath>0</imath> is the units digit of the month, then the other two slots must both be <imath>1</imath>. If <imath>0</imath> is the tens digit of the month, then the other two slots can be either both <imath>1</imath> or both <imath>2</imath>. In total, there are <imath>4</imath> successes here. 
	
Summing through all cases, there are <imath>2 + 3 + 4 = \boxed{\textbf{(E)}~9}</imath> dates. 
 		
-Benedict T (countmath1)

-Edits by Cat_Of_Logic

==Solution 3==
We start with <imath>2023----</imath> we need an extra <imath>0</imath> and an extra <imath>3</imath>. So we have at least one of those extras in the days, except we can have the month <imath>03</imath>. We now have <imath>6</imath> possible months <imath>01,02,03,10,11,12</imath>. For month <imath>1</imath> we have two cases, we now have to add in another 1, and the possible days are <imath>13,31</imath>. For month <imath>2</imath> we need an extra <imath>2</imath> so we can have the day <imath>23</imath> note that we can't use <imath>32</imath> because it is to large. Now for month <imath>3</imath> we can have any number and multiply it by <imath>11</imath> so we have the solution <imath>11,22</imath>. For October we need a <imath>1</imath> and a <imath>3</imath> so we have <imath>13,31</imath> as our choices. For November we have two choices which are <imath>03,30</imath>.Now for December we have <imath>0</imath> options. Summing <imath>2+1+2+2+2</imath> we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)}~9}</imath> solutions.

~kyogrexu
